blogs.title: The 'Update' Doctrine: How Agencies Can Sustain Long-Pending FOIA Withholdings Without New Investigations
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit's reasoning regarding the temporal validity of Exemption 7(A) claims. Specifically, it examines how the court allowed the FBI to satisfy its burden of proving 'pending or reasonably anticipated' proceedings through a relatively brief 'update' declaration (by Joseph Bender) rather than requiring a fresh, detailed evidentiary showing after a multi-year gap. The article discusses the tension between the requirement for specificity in FOIA affidavits and the practical realities of maintaining national security secrecy over long litigation periods, questioning whether this approach lowers the threshold for sustaining indefinite withholdings.

blogs.title: The Ex Parte Shield: Reconciling Due Process Concerns with National Security Deference in FOIA Litigation
blogs.description: Focusing on procedural fairness, this commentary explores the appellate court's acceptance of extensive reliance on ex parte, sealed declarations to resolve both the 'persistence' of an investigation and the issue of document segregability. The post contrasts Farahi's inability to cross-examine or meaningfully rebut these classified assertions with the court's deferential stance toward executive branch expertise in counterterrorism matters. It evaluates whether the current framework effectively neutralizes a plaintiff's ability to test the government's factual predicates when national security is invoked, and what implications this holds for future FOIA challenges involving sensitive intelligence files.

blogs.title: 'Interspersed Line-by-Line': The High Bar for Segregability in Massive Counterterrorism Files
blogs.description: This piece dissects the court's rejection of Farahi's argument that some non-exempt information must exist within his massive 10,000-page file. By reaffirming that random intermingling of exempt and non-exempt text does not constitute 'reasonable segregability,' the opinion reinforces a strict standard that favors total redaction in complex law enforcement contexts. The post analyzes how this interpretation interacts with FOIA's core mandate to maximize disclosure, arguing that it creates a functional immunity for large-scale investigative files where even minor unclassified snippets are deemed inseparable from their classified counterparts due to context.
